intervals.label: construction
intervals.note: End 1990: "The 100km2 wide area air shower detector, AGASA, was completed at Akeno." (same chronology, Heisei 2).
intervals.quote: The construction of the 100km2 wide-area air shower detector, AGASA, started at the Akeno Observatory.

intervals.label: operation
intervals.note: The AGASA results page gives the data epoch of the published spectrum as "Feb. 17, 1990 -- Jul. 31, 2002". Sokolsky & Thomson give "Full operation of the array began in 1993"; Anchordoqui et al. (hep-ph/0206072) say "The full AGASA experiment has been running since 1992"; see the log.
intervals.quote: The AGASA had been in operation as the world's largest air-shower array for 13 years since 1990, but was terminated in January 2004

intervals.label: operation ended
intervals.note: Start is the termination month; observation was handed over to Telescope Array.

name: AGASA
notes: The Akeno Observatory page names Telescope Array as AGASA's successor ("larger scale hybrid successor Telescope Array (TA)"); the lineage row (predecessor) is on experiment:telescope-array.
Start of full operation is stated as 1990 (ICRR), 1992 (Anchordoqui et al.) and 1993 (Sokolsky & Thomson); the ICRR chronology is the operating institute's own and is used.

physics_goals.quote: to study origin of extremely high energy cosmic rays.
physics_goals.value: Study the origin of extremely high energy cosmic rays.

summary.plain: AGASA was a 100-square-kilometre field of 111 particle detectors in the mountains of Japan. Running from 1990 to 2004, it recorded giant cosmic-ray air showers and reported cosmic rays above the expected energy cutoff.
summary.technical: Akeno Giant Air Shower Array: 111 surface scintillators (2.2 m2 each, about 1 km spacing) over about 100 km2 plus 27 shielded muon detectors; hosted at the Akeno Observatory. 1990-2004; reported eight events above 1020 eV and an energy spectrum extending past the GZK energy (Takeda et al. 1998, 2003).
